title: Trusting the Beep, Explained
subtitle: Iben Chikere, Mirela Hanke and Casimir Beng on whether shoppers who say they trust a self-checkout's error prompt override it any less
summary: A research explainer from the School of Emergent Priorities on Iben Chikere, Mirela Hanke and Casimir Beng's poster testing whether shoppers' stated trust in a self-checkout's error prompt predicts their use of the override button. It follows the prompt from the kiosk screen to twelve weeks of till logs and sets the poster's flat chart beside the question it answers. All three authors describe the work in their own words.
topic: A research explainer of the poster testing whether shoppers' stated trust in a self-checkout's item-recognition error prompt predicts how often they press the override button, against twelve weeks of till-linked override logs at four store sites, with a null result

beats.tagline: Stated Confidence in Self-Checkout Error Prompts Does Not Predict Override-Button Use
beats.byline: Iben Chikere, Mirela Hanke and Casimir Beng, School of Emergent Priorities

beats.text: Retailers treat stated confidence in the prompt as a proxy for how shoppers actually use it at the till.
beats.attribution: Chikere, Hanke and Beng, Trusting the Beep

beats.text: Does stated trust move the override hand at all?

beats.label: Override rate by self-reported trust tier

beats.text: Stated trust and the override hand move independently. Confidence in the prompt is not confidence in the till.
We built an instrument to measure something a shopper already does with their hand every week. It turns out the two were never talking to each other.
